propositions.text: Christophe Leuga is a citizen of Cameroon seeking judicial review of a senior immigration officer's January 16, 2020 decision refusing his PRRA application.
The officer concluded Mr. Leuga failed to prove he would face risks under sections 96 and 97 of IRPA if returned to Cameroon.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Christophe Leuga seeks judicial review of a refusal of his PRRA application by a senior immigration officer who found he failed to prove risk under IRPA sections 96 and 97.

propositions.text: Mr. Leuga does not challenge the PRRA officer's merits findings but alleges two procedural fairness breaches at his hearing.
The determinative issue is Mr. Leuga's representation at the hearing convened by the officer.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges two procedural fairness breaches but the court identifies the key issue as Mr. Leuga's representation at the hearing.

propositions.text: Mr. Leuga demonstrated fundamental problems with his representation's competency affecting his procedural fairness rights.
The court will allow the judicial review application based on these findings.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds fundamental problems with Mr. Leuga's representation and allows the judicial review application.

propositions.text: Mr. Leuga was a boxer with the Cameroon national team and fears returning due to death threats from authorities after complaints about the boxing system.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant states he was a boxer fearing return to Cameroon due to death threats after complaints about the boxing system.

propositions.text: Mr. Leuga alleges an assault at home on March 7, 2016, was stabbed, police threatened him when he tried to complain, and he moved cities before leaving Cameroon.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges assault, police threats, and relocation before leaving Cameroon.

propositions.text: Mr. Leuga left Cameroon for the US on August 12, 2016, claimed asylum, then arrived in Canada on August 7, 2019, and his refugee claim was found ineligible on August 12, 2019.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant left Cameroon for the US, claimed asylum, then came to Canada where his refugee claim was found ineligible.

propositions.text: Mr. Leuga applied for a PRRA with counsel Patrizia Ruscio on August 30, 2019.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant applied for PRRA with counsel on August 30, 2019.

propositions.text: The Barreau du Québec temporarily disbarred Ms. Ruscio for three months starting October 8, 2019, and Mr. Leuga acknowledged receipt on November 18, 2019.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision maker notes Ms. Ruscio was temporarily disbarred and Mr. Leuga acknowledged this.

propositions.text: On November 1, 2019, the PRRA officer sent a notice to appear for a November 20 hearing to the applicant and his representative.
Ms. Ruscio was unable to contact clients and her files were taken by the Barreau; Mr. Leuga picked up his file and received the notice on November 18, 2019.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision maker sent a hearing notice; the applicant retrieved his file and received the notice on November 18, 2019.

propositions.text: Mr. Leuga met Roland Franklin, office staff who said he represented applicants and would get a percentage of legal fees.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant met Roland Franklin who claimed to represent applicants and receive a fee percentage.

propositions.text: The hearing was held November 20, 2019; Mr. Leuga was accompanied by Mr. Franklin, who is neither counsel nor immigration consultant.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision maker held the hearing with Mr. Franklin, who was not counsel or consultant, accompanying the applicant.

propositions.text: On November 29, 2019, the officer sent a letter to Mr. Leuga stating Ms. Ruscio was not an authorized representative and invited him to proceed alone or select a new representative.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision maker informed the applicant Ms. Ruscio was unauthorized and invited him to proceed alone or choose a new representative.

propositions.text: On January 16, 2020, the officer issued a negative decision finding Mr. Leuga's fear not plausible or well-founded due to inconsistencies and lack of proof of persecution in Bafang.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision maker found the applicant's fear not plausible and issued a negative decision on January 16, 2020.

propositions.text: Mr. Leuga argues the officer breached procedural fairness by not confirming the qualifications and competency of his representative, Mr. Franklin.
He says holding the hearing while his counsel was suspended was problematic and Mr. Franklin lacked ability and competency to represent him.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the officer breached procedural fairness by not verifying Mr. Franklin's qualifications and holding the hearing with suspended counsel.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness issues require the court to determine fairness of procedure considering all circumstances, not a standard of review analysis.

paragraphs.summary: The court states procedural fairness issues require assessing fairness of procedure considering all circumstances.

propositions.text: The PRRA hearing was November 20, 2019; the officer was unaware of Ms. Ruscio's temporary disbarment at that time, which Mr. Leuga does not dispute.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer was unaware of Ms. Ruscio's disbarment at the hearing, undisputed by the applicant.

propositions.text: Mr. Leuga was accompanied by Mr. Franklin, who is neither counsel nor consultant; Mr. Leuga met him on November 18, 2019, after retrieving his file.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Mr. Franklin accompanied the applicant and is neither counsel nor consultant; they met November 18, 2019.

propositions.text: Mr. Leuga relied on the IRCC PRRA hearing guide stating officers must confirm a signed Use of Representative form and counsel's role is supportive and important.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant relies on IRCC guidelines requiring officers to confirm representation and describing counsel's supportive role.

propositions.text: The court agrees counsel support is vital here as the PRRA is the only consideration of alleged risks in Canada for Mr. Leuga.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds counsel support vital because PRRA is the only consideration of alleged risks for the applicant in Canada.

propositions.text: The hearing transcript shows the officer did not ask Mr. Franklin if he was lawyer or consultant, nor confirm change in counsel or required form on file.
The transcript refers to Mr. Franklin as representative, consultant, and counsel, noting he replaced Ms. Ruscio who was absent.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer did not verify Mr. Franklin's status and the transcript inconsistently refers to him as representative, consultant, and counsel.

propositions.text: Mr. Franklin failed to explain his presence at the hearing and did not mention Ms. Ruscio's disbarment or his late involvement.
Transcript suggests Mr. Franklin told the officer he was filling in for Ms. Ruscio, who was 'unavailable'.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Mr. Franklin failed to explain his presence and said he was filling in for Ms. Ruscio, who was unavailable.

propositions.text: On Nov 29, 2019, the officer sent a Letter to Mr. Leuga noting Ms. Ruscio was not an authorized representative.
The officer informed Mr. Leuga he could proceed without a representative or designate another by submitting a new form.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the officer sent a letter to Mr. Leuga about Ms. Ruscio's unauthorized status and options to proceed or designate another representative.

propositions.text: The officer sent the Letter by email but used an incorrect email address.
Mr. Leuga filed an affidavit about the typographical error causing him not to receive the Letter before the negative decision.
The respondent does not dispute the facts about the email error and Mr. Leuga's lack of notice.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the officer's email error prevented Mr. Leuga from receiving the Letter; the respondent does not dispute this fact.

propositions.text: Mr. Leuga submits his PRRA file was poorly prepared and lacked competent representation.
Ms. Ruscio's PRRA submissions were only two pages; no additional submissions addressed officer's concerns.
At hearing, Mr. Leuga filed handwritten notes considered inconsistent by the officer.
Mr. Leuga believes a competent representative would have filed written submissions post-hearing to clarify inconsistencies.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Leuga argues his PRRA file was poorly prepared with minimal submissions and inconsistent notes, lacking competent representation.

propositions.text: The court finds the record supports Mr. Leuga's argument of inadequate representation.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the record supports Mr. Leuga's claim of inadequate representation.

propositions.text: The Guide recognizes a robust role for representation at PRRA hearings.
Competent representation was particularly important for Mr. Leuga's PRRA application as his only chance to present his case.
Mr. Leuga chose to pursue his application with counsel and could expect competent representation.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Guide values representation, and Mr. Leuga could expect competent counsel for his important PRRA application.

propositions.text: Mr. Leuga arrived with an unprepared file and a representative unfamiliar with his case.
Mr. Leuga was unaware Mr. Franklin was unauthorized; Mr. Franklin did not inform the officer.
The officer failed to follow Guide instructions that would have identified the problem immediately.
The officer tried in good faith to inform Mr. Leuga of the unauthorized status and invite another representative after the hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Mr. Leuga had an unprepared file, unauthorized representative, and the officer failed to follow Guide instructions but tried to inform him later.

propositions.text: The court agrees with Mr. Leuga's counsel that the hearing circumstances were a series of unfortunate events affecting his right to a fair hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees the hearing involved unfortunate events significantly affecting Mr. Leuga's right to a fair hearing.

propositions.text: The court finds Mr. Leuga's right to procedural fairness was violated and allows his judicial review application.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes Mr. Leuga's procedural fairness rights were violated and allows his judicial review application.

propositions.text: The parties did not propose questions for certification, and the court agrees there are none.
The court allows the judicial review application and finds no question of general importance to certify.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes no certification questions were proposed or found and allows the judicial review application.
